L01.text: Four years ago, this was AI video.

L02.text: This is what four years did.

L03.text: In 2022, research labs showed that plain words could become moving pictures.

L04.text: But clips lasted a few seconds, and early animation drew every frame on its own.

L05.text: So faces drifted. Objects melted. Nothing held still.

L06.text: In 2023, Runway's Gen-2 put text-to-video into public hands.

L07.text: Then, in February 2024, OpenAI previewed Sora, promising up to a minute of video.

L08.text: Suddenly, a subject could hold together across a whole shot.

L09.text: The race began. In June 2024 alone, Kling, Luma and Runway all showed new models.

L10.text: By December, Sora was public, and Google's Veo 2 arrived a week later.

L11.text: In May 2025, Veo 3 added generated sound, dialogue included.

L12.text: Then came control: first and last frames, camera moves, and reference images that keep a character consistent.

L13.text: Models even learned to edit real footage, adding, removing or restyling objects, not just inventing it.

L14.text: Video stopped being a slot machine, and started becoming a tool.

L15.text: By September 2026, developers announce thirty-second clips, native 4K, and sound generated with the picture.

L16.text: Light behaves. Shots hold together for seconds, not frames.

L17.text: Even so, Kling's own developers say fingers can warp and text can distort.

L19.text: Now the frame itself is changing. Genie 3 builds worlds you can steer, in real time.

L20.text: Motion was the miracle. Now it's the baseline.

L21.text: From melting pixels... to moving worlds.
